audit: REJECT on one defect, narrow and repairable in a single sentence. insufficientReason describes Ramothloa 2025 (PMC12348877) as 'the second permitted-host review of this species'. audit: The fix is scoped to the sentence, not the evidence base. audit: FABRICATED TABLE CELL — the decisive defect, and it is NEW in this pass. The record now states, twice, that Mtendwa 2026 'assigns [alpha-thujone] to "Leaves, seeds" - both parts, not the leaf alone'. It does not. I pulled the raw HTML of PMC13516395 and extracted the table rows containing 'hujone'. There is exactly one, and its cells are: ['Leaves', 'α-Thujone', 'Essential oil hydrodistillation', 'GC-MS', 'Bioactivity marker; potential toxicity concern', '[69,70]']. The plant-part cell is 'Leaves' alone. The string 'Leaves, seeds' does occur in that table, but it is the plant-part cell of a DIFFERENT row: ['Leaves, seeds', 'Ricinine', 'Methanol, ethanol extraction', 'HPLC, LC-MS', 'Insecticidal, antimicrobial, antioxidant, toxicological marker']. The previous auditor's Rule 1 objection was itself wrong — it read the ricinine row and attributed it to thujone — and the fixer adopted that error verbatim, presenting a cell from one row as a quotation from another. The original record ('tabulates alpha-thujone under leaves') was correct and has now been corrupted. A quoted-and-attributed table cell that belongs to a different analyte is precisely the failure class this audit exists to stop: an AI system extracting this page verbatim would carry a false attribution out of it. Appears in adverseEffects entry 'Alpha-thujone reported as a constituent of leaf and seed essential oil...' (including its effect title, which also now misstates the source) and in the contraindication 'Seizure disorder, or concurrent use of anything that lowers the seizure threshold'. Fix at the root: restore 'Leaves'. If the fixer wants the corroborating point, Mtendwa's table independently assigns RICININE to 'Leaves, seeds', which supports the Worbs ricinine-in-all-parts statement the record already carries — but it must be attributed to the ricinine row, not the thujone row.

audit: SUPPRESSED AUTHOR CHARACTERISATION IN THE AMES ENTRY (Rule 3). Abbas 2018's own abstract states: 'R. communis methanolic extracts revealed mild mutagenicity against TA98 (range 1975 ± 67 to 2628 ± 79 revertant colonies) and TA100 (range 2773 ± 92 to 3461 ± 147 revertant colonies) strains'. The record reports the leaf revertant counts and four limitations, then titles the entry 'data that can be read neither as a positive nor as a clearance' — without ever reporting that the authors themselves characterised their extracts as mildly mutagenic. The record's caution about the missing negative control, the missing S9 arm and the non-significant footnote is well judged and should stay; but the study's own adverse characterisation is a finding it reports, and Rule 3 requires the record to carry it rather than substitute the record's own read of the table. Add the authors' sentence, then keep the limitations that qualify it.

audit: DECISIVE (Rule 11) — three asserted negatives fail on a reproducible search of the permitted hosts. I ran the search the record implies: PubMed for the term 'Godanti' returns 5 records (PMIDs 42161236, 40720339, 39216714, 20532095, 22131712); PMC returns 32. That single search overturns three statements the record makes. (i) adverseEffects[2].note says the Das 2024 in vitro paper 'is the only experimental work in the permitted sources on Godanti Bhasma as a single substance'. PMID 40720339 — Dutt G, Goswami V, Faiz A, Joshi A, Jayanand, Das SK. 'Exploring the Sequential Cellular Events of Phagocytosis Triggered by Godanti Bhasma in Mammalian Cells.' J Vis Exp. 2025 Jul 11;(221), doi 10.3791/68321 — is a second single-substance experimental paper on Godanti Bhasma, indexed on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, a permitted host. The exclusivity claim is false. (ii) adverseEffects[1].note says 'No adverse-event report, poisoning case or pharmacovigilance signal naming Godanti Bhasma was located in the permitted sources.' PMC3271522 (Indian J Pharmacol, Stevens-Johnson syndrome case report) states verbatim: 'Some of the ayurvedic drugs causing adverse drug reactions are guggul, svarnabhasma, ras manikya, godanti, ginko echinacae, St. Johns wort, ginseng, lavanabhaskar, parad preparations etc.' That is a named adverse-reaction attribution on a permitted host. Its weakness is documented in the same permitted corpus and must be carried with it: PMC3371481 is a published letter objecting that 'several drugs like Guggulu, Swarna Bhasma, Rasa Manikya, Godanti, Lavana Bhaskara, and Parada have been described to have adverse drug reactions without proper references.' Either carry both with the dispute stated, or drop the asserted negative — but the record cannot assert that nothing was located. (iii) doseLimits.text opens 'NO DOSE LIMIT FOR GODANTI BHASMA AS A SINGLE INGREDIENT HAS BEEN ESTABLISHED IN ANY PERMITTED SOURCE', and contraindications['Use in children'] says 'No paediatric dose ... for Godanti Bhasma exists in the permitted sources.' PMC11625250 (Proposed clinical algorithm for hematinic bhasmas selection for Ayurvedic pediatric care, J Ayurveda Integr Med) carries Table 1, 'Dosages of bhasmas as per the ayurvedic formulary of India', listing 'Godanti Bhasma 500 mg', and the paper's whole subject is deriving paediatric doses from those adult AFI figures by Young's rule while stating 'Clinical research for Bhasma's paediatric doses is highly warranted.' A single-ingredient AFI dose figure for this exact substance sits on a permitted host. This is precisely the Rule 11 failure class: 'I found nothing' written up as 'it does not exist'.

audit: NEW DEFECT (blocking), PMC12386474 Table 4. The record still reports platelets as the ONLY haematological exception in the acute arm. The paper's own Table 4 marks two further significant differences in the untreated-seed (CB) group at 2000 mg/kg: MCV 52.20 +/- 0.54 (b) versus control 53.84 +/- 0.27 (a), and MCH 18.04 +/- 0.11 (b) versus control 18.50 +/- 0.11 (a), the legend stating 'different superscript letters indicate significant differences at p < 0.05'. Both are decreases in the untreated-seed group and both are absent from the record. The record instead repeats the paper's prose claim ('except for platelets (PLT), which showed a statistically significant difference') without noting that the paper's own table contradicts it, while positively enumerating what WAS normal (differentials, the nine serum-biochemistry parameters). A clinician or AI system reading this record would conclude platelets were the sole haematological abnormality. That is the same class of defect the last audit rejected, one layer deeper.
audit: Fetched and read all seven cited sources in raw form (not via summariser) and re-derived every table value. All URLs are on permitted hosts.

audit: BLOCKING - Rule 1 / dropped hazard, Narula et al. (PMC12554104). The record states Kahrva pishti was 'one of twelve concurrent preparations ... of which six were metallic or mineral' and lists 'Tab Cytocruel AT twice daily' among the remaining six non-metallic items, in heavyMetals, in the adverseEffects note and in the concurrent-bhasma contraindication. The paper states verbatim: 'The herbo-mineral formulation CYTOCRUEL which is a propretiary medicine contains drugs from different herbs viz., Cinnamomumspp., Boerhavia spp., Capsicum spp., Moringa spp., Curcuma Spp; Glycyrrhiza spp., Tecomella Spp. and Syzygium spp. Metals including copper, mercury, and sulphur are also present.' The source therefore documents at least SEVEN metal-bearing co-administered products, one of them mercury-containing, and the record files the mercury-containing one on the non-metal side of a count it presents as derived from the source. A documented mercury co-exposure in the only human exposure on record appears nowhere in the record. This is the same defect the previous auditor blocked on (understating the co-administered load in the passage whose whole purpose is the confounding/co-exposure argument); the fixer corrected the total from six to twelve but left the misclassification, so the objection was papered over rather than fixed at its root.

audit: STATED SEARCH DOES NOT REPRODUCE, AND THE NEGATIVE IS FALSE (decisive). insufficientReason claims 'Two indexed sources describing Strychnos potatorum itself were located' and 'no genotoxicity, carcinogenicity or reproductive-toxicity testing of this species was located', after naming PubMed/PMC among the hosts searched. I ran that search: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Strychnos+potatorum%22 reports 37 results, not two, and the first page of results contains Neelamkavil SV, Thoppil JE. 'Genotoxic assessment of calcium hypochlorite and Strychnos potatorum Linn. seeds-two commonly used water purifying agents.' Rev Environ Health. 2015;30(1):19-23, PMID 25411981 - a genotoxicity assessment of this species' seeds, on a permitted host, surfaced by the most obvious possible query. This is the rule 11 failure class verbatim: 'I found nothing' converted into 'no such testing exists'.

audit: OMITTED SPECIES-SPECIFIC ADVERSE FINDING FROM A PERMITTED HOST. That 2015 paper reports, in the Allium cepa chromosome aberration assay, a dose-dependent reduction in mitotic index and increase in abnormality percentage, with S. potatorum seeds expressing 'mild cytotoxicity' while the genotoxic effect was 'negligible when compared with positive control'. A mild-cytotoxicity finding for this species' seeds is an adverse finding and must be carried with its assay system and its limitations (plant cytogenetic model, water-purification context, not a mammalian genotoxicity battery). Instead the record asserts a blanket absence of genotoxicity data and, in adverseEffects[1] note (7), leans on that absence.

audit: VERDICT: reject. The two previously-flagged Angers method errors and the Brown arm-merging are genuinely fixed at the root, the ayush.gov.in method statement is now true and reproduces, and the severity ordering is resolved. But the Saper repair introduced a NEW and worse defect than the one it replaced, and a second selective-quotation problem in the Angers block survived both prior passes unexamined. Both are Rule 1. audit: PRIMARY (Rule 1, new defect introduced by this repair) - Saper 2008 (PMC2755247). The previous auditor's objection was that 'Saper's stated limitations are that...' asserted completeness while listing three of five. The fixer's remedy was to escalate the completeness claim to 'Saper states five limitations, and all five are recorded here' - and the five it then lists are NOT the paper's five. I pulled the limitations paragraph verbatim. It reads: 'Limitations of our study include potential misclassification of the product's country of manufacture and rasa shastra status... Unobtainable products were not random... We did not assess batch-to-batch variability in metal concentrations... Wide variation among published standards for acceptable limits of daily metal ingestion makes it difficult to assess the magnitude of potential toxicity for different products. Finally, we did not ascertain the specific physical form or chemical species of the metals.' That is the author-enumerated set, closed by 'Finally'. The record drops the fourth item (wide variation among published standards) entirely and substitutes the internet-purchase generalizability sentence, which sits elsewhere in the Discussion and is not part of that paragraph. So the record omits a stated limitation while affirmatively certifying that none is omitted.

audit: BLOCKING - the record makes a false statement about what a cited study did and found. heavyMetals says of Joshi 2015: 'it reports no lead, mercury or arsenic screening and no toxicity testing, and its own conclusion is limited to "fingerprinting of MB prepared using a particular method".' I fetched the full text (PMC4623633, the PMC version of PMID 26600667) this session. The paper carries 'Table 8. Composition of heavy metals in different samples of MB detected by EDAX method' and states in its discussion: 'Heavy metals such as As, Hg, Cd, Pd were detected below the permissible limits [Table 8]. Hence, MB prepared by the method followed in the study is not only quite safe, but also a natural source that provides essential micronutrients on internal administration.' Its full-text CONCLUSION section, which the record does not quote, reads in part: 'Presence of essential micronutrients and permissible limits of heavy metals proves the compound to be safe as well as efficacious for internal administration.' So the study did screen for arsenic, mercury, cadmium and lead, and it did draw a safety conclusion; the record denies both. This is the same failure class the previous auditor blocked on (an unverified assertion about a study's methods), and the fixer's claim that it 're-verified at source' every previously-clean item did not catch it, because only the PubMed abstract was read. The correct repair is not to delete the sentence but to report what Joshi actually claims and then say why it cannot be relied on: EDAX is a semi-quantitative surface technique whose detection limits are orders of magnitude above the microgram-per-gram levels at issue, so 'below permissible limits by EDAX' is not evidence of compliance - exactly the argument the record already makes correctly for Balkrishna's EDX. Suppressing a source's own safety claim is as much a misrepresentation as amplifying it, and a record built to be quoted verbatim by clinicians and AI systems cannot tell a reader that a cited paper contains no heavy-metal data when it contains a table of it.

audit: BLOCKING - Rule 2, methodological detail attributed to a study that does not state it, and the record contradicts itself two sentences later. heavyMetals opens: 'Balkrishna 2025 (J Ethnopharmacol) synthesized Mukta Pishti (MKP) from marine pearls following the classical Rasatarangini methodology and characterized it using...'. The paper does not say the authors synthesized the test article. The abstract's ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE sentence is a general description of the medicine - 'Mukta Pishti (MKP) is a traditional Ayurvedic medicine described in classical textbook Rasatarangini and synthesized from marine pearls following classical methodology' - not a methods statement, and the phrase 'Rasatarangini methodology' is the record's own splice of two separate clauses. The competing-interest statement, which the record itself quotes further down, says the opposite about provenance: 'Mukta Pisthi was sourced from Divya Pharmacy, Haridwar, Uttarakhand, India... Other than supplying the test article, Divya Pharmacy was not involved in any aspect of the research stated in this study.' Attributing the preparation of the test article to the investigators is a provenance claim of the same kind as the 'single commercial batch' invention that got this record rejected last time, and it materially changes how a reader weighs the characterization data. Fix: state that the study characterized a test article supplied by Divya Pharmacy, and if the classical-methodology sentence is carried, quote it as the paper's description of the medicine ('synthesized from marine pearls following classical methodology'), as the adverseEffects mollusc entry already does correctly.

audit: BLOCKING (Rule 12, denominator) - Saper 2004 median lead is attached to the wrong denominator. The record states: '14 (20 percent) contained heavy metals, and among those 14 the median lead concentration was 40 micrograms per gram with a range of 5 to 37,000 micrograms per gram.' The source (PMID 15598918, abstract retrieved verbatim via NCBI efetch) reads: 'A total of 14 (20%) of 70 HMPs (95% confidence interval, 11%-31%) contained heavy metals: lead (n = 13; median concentration, 40 microg/g; range, 5-37,000), mercury (n = 6; median concentration, 20,225 microg/g; range, 28-104,000), and/or arsenic (n = 6; median concentration, 430 microg/g; range, 37-8130).' The median of 40 ug/g is over the 13 products CONTAINING LEAD, not over the 14 products containing heavy metals. This is precisely the failure class Rule 12 names, and the fixer's own change-note asserts it applied Rule 12 here ('tied to the 14 of 70 products that contained heavy metals') - it tied it to the wrong number. The same sentence's mercury (n=6, median 20,225 ug/g, max 104,000) and arsenic (n=6, median 430 ug/g, max 8,130) figures, which are far more alarming than the lead figure the record kept, are dropped entirely, as is the abstract's finding that 'If taken as recommended by the manufacturers, each of these 14 could result in heavy metal intakes above published regulatory standards.' Fix: state 'n=13 products containing lead' verbatim, and carry the mercury and arsenic medians and the regulatory-exceedance sentence alongside.

audit: BLOCKING (Rules 1 and 3) - Joshi 2016's haematological adverse findings are missing, and the conclusion is truncated while the record asserts it is complete. I retrieved PMC4850776 in full. The Discussion states: 'None of the groups showed any effect on W.B.C. and platelet count except for their raised levels at 10 T.D.' and the authors' own reading of it: 'Increased WBC count is indicative of inflammatory conditions of certain organs, especially of liver.' The abstract Conclusion reads in two sentences: 'Lauha Bhasma was found to be safe at the therapeutic dose and also at five times the therapeutic dose levels. However, alteration in some of the biochemical and haematological parameters along with histopathological findings were evident at the highest dose level.' The record carries only the first sentence of that conclusion, carries no haematological finding anywhere, and then claims in its own note: 'The paper's conclusion is carried in full rather than only its reassuring half.' That claim is false - the adverse clause of the conclusion is exactly what was cut, and the raised WBC and platelet counts at 10 TD appear nowhere in the record. This is the Rule 1 truncation pattern (stopping a quoted conclusion immediately before its adverse closing clause) compounded by an explicit assertion of completeness. Fix: add the WBC/platelet elevation at 10 TD with the authors' inflammatory interpretation, and quote the conclusion's second sentence.

audit: SOURCES FETCHED AND CHECKED MYSELF, not taken from the fixer: PubMed efetch for 37054826, 29528276, 33881010, 18728265, 15598918, 36179284, 37492071, 29960971; PMC6060866 full text including Table 2, its footnotes b/c/d and the Table 3 paragraph; PMC2755247 for the Saper 2008 correction notice; PubMed esearch for JAMA 300:1652; the live FDA and NCCIH pages. audit: BLOCKING - rule 11. heavyMetals.text ends 'None of these class-level reports tested Nityananda Rasa itself.' I checked each one: Mikulski's published tables give only Table 3's nine highest-content product families (Indukantham, Brihat Vatchintamani Ras, Swarna Bhasma, Saubhagya, Shulagna, Arbudari) and never enumerate the 252 samples, so the paper cannot support that claim; Ciocan's implicated preparation is unnamed ('One of the two drugs contained extremely high concentrations of lead and mercury'); Hardin's published abstract is four sentences of general advice with no product named; Hore reports 584 aggregated remedies. This is 'I found nothing' rewritten as 'I confirmed it was never tested', in a record that a clinician or an AI system will quote. Everything else in that paragraph is correctly hedged, which makes this one sentence more misleading, not less.

audit: PRIMARY DEFECT (introduced by this repair). The record applies Panigrahi et al.'s significance markers rigorously where they exculpate and the narrative text where it incriminates, and never discloses that the two disagree. It correctly states 'The triglyceride, VLDL-cholesterol and alkaline phosphatase increases at TED x 10 were therefore NON-SIGNIFICANT' by reading the @ markers in Table 4. But it then asserts, in the `frequency` field of the 28-day entry and again in the note ('at TED itself the paper still reports a significant increase in relative uterus weight and significant decreases in triglyceride and VLDL-cholesterol'), three flat significant findings at TED that carry NO @ marker anywhere in the same tables. Verified at HTML-cell level: Triglyceride row = 135.60±12.97 | 97.10±9.84 | 129.20±12.51 | 177.89±29.55 | 140.70±20.53, no marker in any column; VLDL-cholesterol row = 27.10±2.54 | 19.40±1.96 | 25.80±2.51 | 35.89±5.96 | 28.10±4.14, no marker; Table 3 Uterus row = 230.70±42.29 | 346.50±20.78 | 319.67±28.89 | 300.78±26.33, no marker. In Table 3 the @ markers sit on Seminal vesicles at TED x 5 (704.37±18.21 @) and on Liver at TED x 10(R) (2.919±34.95 @) — NOT on liver at TED x 5, which is what the narrative sentence the record quotes actually claims. In Table 4 the only @ in the whole table is serum calcium at TED x 10 and TED x 10(R).

audit: REJECT on one defect, newly introduced by this pass, in the exact failure class the record was rejected for last time. insufficientReason states: 'the same five terms against db=pmc returned five distinct articles in total, PMC11705355, PMC4279319, PMC3841994, PMC3331427 and PMC6631742.' I re-ran all five terms against https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pmc. Actual returns: 'Vatagajankusha' Count 4 (11705355, 4279319, 3841994, 3331427); 'Vatagajankush' Count 1 (4279319); 'Vatagajankusa' Count 2 (6631742, 3331427); 'Vatagajendra' Count 0; and 'Vata gajankusha' Count 3 (11663963, 10267528, 3215365). That is eight distinct articles, not five. I tested the two-word term both ways, as --data-urlencode 'term="Vata gajankusha"' and as 'term=Vata gajankusha'; both return the same Count 3 and the same three IDs, so the discrepancy is not an encoding artefact. The record's own framing is 'Searches actually run, stated so that they reproduce' - and this one does not.

audit: The three omitted articles are PMC11663963 (Brahmi vati and Aswagandharista in major depressive disorder), PMC10267528 (Ayurveda in psychotic disorders, systematic review) and PMC3215365 (Panchakarma therapy and Unmada Gajankusha Rasa in major depressive disorder). They concern Unmada Gajankusha Rasa, a different preparation, so no hazard is being concealed and the substantive insufficientData finding still looks right. The defect is the falsifiable claim, not the safety conclusion: a clinician or AI system re-running the search the record publishes gets a result set the record says does not exist, and the record's negative assertion is scoped to 'the other four' when the stated search returns seven others. Rule 11 is categorical on this point.
